extracted.intended_audience: math olympiad students and problem solvers (USAMO/IMO/contest participants) and students learning how to write proofs
extracted.subtask_description: Advice for composing clear, correct, and grader-friendly mathematical proofs and contest write-ups, with competition-specific notes for olympiad settings (USAMO/IMO). Emphasizes correctness, structure, presentation, and checking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Never write wrong math
rubrics_metrics.description: This is much more of a math issue than a style issue: you can lose all of your points for making false claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not make egregiously false claims; the grader may stop reading. Do not state something only partially true and 'fix it later' — at best it annoys graders and at worst confuses them. Examples of ways to lose points include flipping an inequality sign, misunderstanding definitions (e.g. what 'function' means), making unjustified assumptions, stating key assertions without proof, making logical errors, or missing cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasize the point where you cross the ocean
rubrics_metrics.description: Highlight the few key ideas of the solution so graders immediately see the high-level approach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Isolate crucial steps as standalone parts; introduce and label the main idea explicitly (e.g. 'the key observation'); display and, if useful, number important equations/claims so the reader can glance and understand the approach. Use explicit statements like 'the crucial claim is X' or 'the main idea is Y'. This telegraphs the heart of the solution and separates 'big ideas' from routine checking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure for 'find all' and 'find the minimum/maximum' problems
rubrics_metrics.description: When a problem asks to 'find all' or 'find min/max', follow a clear three-part structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For 'find all' problems: (1) start 'We claim the answer is ...'; (2) prove these candidates satisfy the condition (plug back in); (3) prove these are the only ones. For min/max: (1) 'We claim the minimum/maximum is ...'; (2) prove it is attainable (give construction); (3) prove the bound (lower/upper bound). Always include the verification even if trivial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leave space
rubrics_metrics.description: Use whitespace and visual layout to improve readability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Skip lines after paragraphs, put isolated lemmas/claims on their own line with whitespace before/after, split casework into separate paragraphs or bullet points, display important equations (use aligned displays for long calculations) rather than squeezing them into inline text. Visual separation helps graders parse long solutions quickly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include a diagram if you needed one
rubrics_metrics.description: If you used a diagram to solve the problem, provide it to the reader as part of your solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In contests, submit the diagram you drew while solving (add headers). Don't expect the grader to reconstruct your diagram — a small typo in a definition can make their drawing different from yours and ruin comprehension. This applies beyond classical geometry: any problem where a visual aid was used should include it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pay special attention to definitions (extra important)
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions must be complete and correct because readers cannot 'fix' incorrect definitions the way they might fix a minor arithmetic slip.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write definitions in complete sentences, give examples when a definition is nontrivial, consider naming repeatedly used objects (so you don't repeatedly write 'the set of bad numbers'), and ensure your definition fully specifies the object/algorithm. Avoid writing 'worst case' casually unless you precisely justify it. Naming objects can help reveal missing definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other presentation and practical tips
rubrics_metrics.description: Various small but important practical habits that improve write-ups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Have neat handwriting, leave ~1-inch margins, write proofs forwards even if you solved them backwards, clearly indicate when you cite a theorem and how, choose sensible variable names, and neatly strike out unwanted parts (don't scribble). These small habits make solutions easier to grade and reduce mistakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write concisely via organization (for intermediate students)
rubrics_metrics.description: Conciseness is often achieved by reorganizing and planning, not merely deleting text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organize proofs into a tight sequence of discrete claims, split cases neatly (bullets), and write logical steps forwards rather than backwards. Prefer 'X implies Y thus Z' to convoluted backward reasoning. Rewriting for structure yields concise and readable solutions rather than simple cuts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Display and number key claims/equations
rubrics_metrics.description: Important equations or equivalences should be displayed and can be numbered for reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Putting central identities or claims on their own display (and optionally numbering them) helps the grader find and reuse them later in your solution — especially useful in functional equations and long algebraic manipulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: How much detail to include
rubrics_metrics.description: Include enough detail to convince the grader you solved the problem; not more is required purely to fill space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You lose points if a student who did NOT solve the problem could have written the same words. Avoid unexplained phrases like 'it's easy to see X' unless the justification is obvious to any solver; when in doubt, give enough justification or outline the reasoning so the grader can tell you understand it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citing lemmas
rubrics_metrics.description: It's usually acceptable to cite known results that are named and do not trivialize the problem; for others, provide an outline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you cite a lemma outside of that scope, outline a short proof to show you could write it out; you don't need to give the full detailed proof of a well-known result but include a couple lines of the idea to demonstrate validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common ways to 'fake-solve' and lose points
rubrics_metrics.description: Typical mistakes that make a solution wrong/incomplete despite appearing plausible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common pitfalls: flipping inequality signs, not understanding central definitions (e.g. what 'function' means), making intuitive but unjustified assumptions, stating key assertions without proof, committing logical errors (pointwise traps), missing cases or possibilities, and failing to do both directions in 'find all' problems. These are responsible for most lost points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Olympiad grading (unspoken rubric)
rubrics_metrics.description: The informal scoring categories used by many olympiad graders (score is integer 0–7).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical unspoken rubric: 7* = problem solved; 6 = tiny slip (repairable); 5 = small gap or non-central mistake; 2 = lots of genuine progress; 1 = significant non-trivial progress; 0* = 'busy work', special cases, lots of writing. (Default starred values noted.) In theory grading is based on math alone, but style affects readability and thus can affect scoring indirectly.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to check your solutions during the year
rubrics_metrics.description: A practical three-step algorithm for self-checking practice solutions using peers and online resources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Step 1: write up neatly to help spot your own mistakes; reorganize and simplify as you write. Step 2: compare your draft to the Art of Problem Solving forum thread, especially reputable users, to sanity-check approach and find the 'ocean-crossing' point where differences may indicate a mistake. Step 3: post your final draft on the thread for feedback (Cunningham's Law will surface blatant errors).

rubrics_metrics.name: How to check your solutions during a contest
rubrics_metrics.description: During contest conditions you must develop the ability to check solutions independently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The principal advice is to 'write clearly and carefully' — the act of writing often reveals flaws in your solution. Cultivate habits through practice so that you can detect conceptual gaps without external feedback; checking during write-up is frequently where contestants discover mistakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use examples when defining complicated objects
rubrics_metrics.description: When a definition is nontrivial, accompany it with examples to aid understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples often communicate the idea more clearly than the formal definition alone. Provide explicit illustrative instances to make the definition concrete for the grader/reader.
